html:
Before the details, here it is in one sentence: talk to Germans as much as you can, however bad your German is.

My favorite picture on the subject: “Forget about pronunciation! The only way to stop being embarrassed is to say it. Say it out loud: F**k, F**k!!!” [From Diors Man, a Chinese web comedy series]

In four years in Germany I got as far as B2, then slid back to B1 after I stopped taking classes. I never sat a German exam. I improved through classes and, far more, through talking to Germans, so my German simply grew wild. I never reached working proficiency, but everyday conversation is no problem: I took my driving test in German, taught lab classes to German students, and can discuss basic academic questions. So I think I fit what the asker is after: not the way German is taught in China, where you study it and still can’t speak it, but fast progress in speaking, plus a grasp of both the language and the country.

My German when I arrived: a vocabulary of Hallo, Danke, Bitte, Ich heiße xxx, Ich komme aus China, in other words lesson one of A1 in Xinqiujing, a standard German textbook in China. For everything else I relied on English. I had also sneaked into a German class that Volkswagen ran for its new hires, and got dirty looks for it, and I knew a little basic grammar.

I’ve been interested in languages since I was a kid, so before coming to Germany I quietly resolved not only to learn German properly but to make German friends! (Sometimes naive... I did make some in the end, but it was a long, complicated process, and painful at first. I kept asking myself: why is he/she treating me like this? What on earth did I do wrong???) I even made a bold vow: I would defend my PhD in German! In the end I did it in English, but I know that if I’d been willing to put in the preparation, a German defense would have been fine. Only the Q&A would have got a bit embarrassing...

Our institute was fairly small, without many foreigners, so German’s place as the working language was unshakable. My very first group meeting put me firmly in my place. Everyone reported on their past week. Everyone before me spoke German; when it got to me, my boss switched to English, I introduced myself, everyone gave me a very warm welcome, and then they slipped back into German mode as smoothly as you like... This went on until my fourth year: just when my German was good enough to follow what they were saying, the group meetings switched to English, because by then there were more foreigners... Still, that’s not extreme by German standards. You can survive in Germany with English, but without German you’ll keep hitting walls and getting looked down on in daily life. The loop I kept getting stuck in went like this:

Scene one

“How long have you been in Germany?”

“A couple of months.”

“Oh, then I guess you have learned some German?”

“Yeah... I am in a German course.”

“Ah, dann können wir auf Deutsch sprechen.”

“Ja klar...”

“flkdahfjdksalhfdsahfdsafdlkjafdafd.................”

Scene two

“Excuse me, could you speak English?”

“Nein, nur Deutsch.”

“................”

So if you want to stand on your own two feet, there’s nothing for it but to slog away at German. Enough rambling; let’s get down to business.

====================

===== The method =====

====================

In short, my method for learning German was:

1. Take German classes that focus on speaking — 2. Write down every common spoken word and expression you come across — 3. Use them right away when you chat with Germans

Step three matters most, because however you study and however many words you memorize, there’s only one goal in the end: communication. One more thing worth knowing: most Germans love to teach. They have an innate sense that their language is superior, so when they see a foreigner working hard to learn it, they’re very happy to help. Actually, this isn’t just about languages or about Germans: most people won’t turn away someone who is making an effort to try something new.

1. I took classes in three places: the university, the Volkshochschule (a community adult-education center) and Inlingua. Since I had a tiny bit of German before arriving, the university’s A1.1 class felt slow, so I signed up at Inlingua as well, though again starting from A1. After a few lessons that still felt slow, so I jumped to A1.2. Keeping up was a bit of a struggle but manageable, so I stayed. After cramming vocabulary and grammar in my own time for a while, I could follow comfortably. I dropped the university course after one semester. When I’d finished A1 at Inlingua, I went to the Volkshochschule for A2.1, which moved at about the same pace as the university; I coasted through a semester there and went back to Inlingua. This time I bit the bullet and signed up for an intensive course: four hours a day, five days a week, a bit over 300 euros a month. My research project suffered somewhat during that time, but I improved fast. In two months I reached B2, skipping another level along the way.

Of the three, I recommend Inlingua above all, because it was the only one that focused on speaking rather than on exercises, grammar or exams. If you’re aiming for TestDaF or DSH, of course, that’s a different story. Classes are small, around ten people, and every lesson involves lots of interaction and conversation with the teacher, which is the whole idea behind Inlingua. I’ve heard the Sprachenakademie works in a similar way, but I didn’t take enough of their classes to judge.

As for using the textbook, look up every word you don’t know and add it to a vocabulary list. I recommend Dehelper, a German–Chinese dictionary app. I paid a bit over 60 yuan for a membership so I could sync my word list between my phone and my computer. Point two below covers how to memorize words.

Besides language classes, most universities run language-partner programs, and there are similar groups on Facebook. Also, speak German with your international classmates as much as you can. I met lots of foreign friends in my German classes; everyone’s German was terrible, so there was no pressure. You don’t learn as much as you would from Germans, but it’s great practice for expressing yourself, and for your confidence. With other foreigners you mostly practice speaking; with Germans you mostly practice listening and learn to say things idiomatically. And more important than learning the language for its own sake, I made a lot of friends. We’d get together and shoot the breeze whenever we had time, and escaping the slightly dour German atmosphere felt great.

2. Beyond the words in the textbook, collect every new word you meet in daily life: in German emails, on all the signs and labels in supermarkets and shops, in conversations with Germans. These are bound to be common, high-frequency words. Put them in your word list and go over it again and again. Since you also keep running into them in daily life, this repeated exposure makes them stick quickly, and they find their way into how you speak. Back then, whenever I had a spare moment I studied words and reviewed my list: on the bus, before bed, on the toilet. Scraps of time are perfect for language learning, and they don’t eat into the big blocks of time you need for research. One thing that kept me interested: a word you added to your list an hour ago might turn up in a conversation with Germans the next hour, so it sticks even faster, and that feels like a real achievement.

Dehelper doesn’t always give accurate, idiomatic translations, so I also used LEO and Wikipedia a lot. Germans tend to use LEO. I used it whenever English–German or German–English translation was involved: for example, when the unfamiliar word was English and had no good Chinese equivalent, Dehelper was no use, and that’s where LEO came in. And for technical terms nothing is more accurate or comprehensive than Wikipedia. With rarer words I sometimes had to triple-check with all three, or with even more tools.

3. The first two points aren’t hard for us Chinese students; anyone can do them if they put in the time and care. The last one, talking to Germans, may not be so easy, especially while your German is still bad and you’re too embarrassed to open your mouth. I’m grateful that my officemate when I first arrived was a language maniac: he also took German classes like crazy and struck up conversations with Germans everywhere. Thanks to him, I thick-skinnedly joined in the awkward small talk too. On the surface his conversations with Germans flowed beautifully; you’d marvel at how much he understood and how well he expressed himself. But actually... his secret was to keep changing the topic, steering the Germans into scenarios he had prepared in advance. Secret number two: keep asking questions, about the language, about the culture, or tell jokes he’d made up himself... I don’t have his appetite for socializing, or his talent for defusing awkwardness, and at the start I overreached by speaking only German and no English, using the handful of German sentences I knew, such as:

In the canteen, after getting my food and taking a bite: “Es schmeckt gut!” (It tastes good!)

On the way back: “Die Sonne scheint!” (The sun is shining!)

And: “Wie heißt xxx auf Deutsch?” (What’s xxx in German?)

.......

At first everyone was quite taken with it, but spend long enough with a twentysomething who talks less fluently than a two-year-old and you can’t help wondering now and then, “Is this guy an idiot?” And when Germans don’t feel like talking, they really do just ignore you... So at the beginning I often felt low and wondered why they were so cold. Looking back, the key is not to get stuck in the Germans’ comfort zone: silence. Germans think nothing of sitting together without saying a word, but most people elsewhere in the world can’t do that, and naturally read it as social awkwardness. (This post is a fun read and may help some people stop blaming themselves for thinking Germans dislike them: German Culture: My Awkward Social Encounters with Germans.) It’s not your fault! And they’re not in a mood, either. They just don’t feel like talking right now, and they’re perfectly comfortable with that...

Insisting on German also cost me many chances to get to know my colleagues and their research more deeply, which I could have done in English. The upside was that my German improved especially fast in the first two years. After a little over six months I could handle basic conversations, and apart from academic topics I spoke German almost all the time. In my third year I started teaching some lab classes in German, and in my fourth year I took my driving test in German, which gave the reading skills of a self-taught learner like me a big boost. For me, the hardest part of the driving test was the 1,500 questions of the theory exam: pure, damn reading comprehension... It’s give and take; weigh up the pros and cons for yourself.

To avoid or defuse awkward small talk with Germans, and learn some German along the way, try starting a conversation by asking questions: about the language, football, culture and so on. Since Germans love to set people straight, they’ll usually explain things to you in great detail, even if their grammar is shakier than yours, haha. Just steer clear of sensitive topics, especially that dark chapter of their history; Germans really avoid it.

In the end my grammar still isn’t solid and I make all kinds of mistakes when I speak, but as long as you dare to speak, Germans will basically get your point. Ranking the four skills from strongest to weakest, mine go: speaking > reading > listening > writing. I don’t need to write research papers in German, so I don’t much mind that writing is my weakest. For more formal emails you can look up templates, and for ordinary emails there’s no real problem as long as the meaning is clear.

Curious about a guy from Northeast China knocking around European academia and industry all these years? See my Zhihu column PhD Diaries, and for acoustics (popular science, curiosities, little-known facts, industrial applications, case studies and where the field is heading) my WeChat Official Account, Ziyu Acoustics.
